title: Cast your care (1 Peter 5:7)
hook: cast all your care on him, for he cares for you

segments.voice: Yesterday, fear not: heaven's word to Abram, Mary and the shepherds, each time with a second half. Your line was fear not. What true thing did you put after the for? Day one thousand three hundred ninety-nine.

A sticky note on the fridge, half hidden under a magnet: the dentist, the rent, the thing with your sister, the noise the car is making. Lists like that have a way of growing. Cross one thing off and two more appear. Near the end of a short letter from Peter, written to Christians going through suffering, there's one sentence aimed at that list. In the King James words: "Casting all your care upon him; for he careth for you." Today: cast your care.

Start with the verb. Cast is not set down politely. It's a throwing word. The same verb turns up in Luke, when the disciples throw their garments onto a colt for Jesus to ride. A physical motion: off you, onto something else. Then the line just before it, because Peter ties the two together: "Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in due time." In this letter, handing over worry is a kind of humility. It's admitting you were never built to carry everything. Next, the picture is older than Peter's letter. Psalm 55 says, "Cast thy burden upon the LORD, and he shall sustain thee." Notice the promise. Not that the burden disappears, but that you'll be held up. Sustained. Then a story that shows the throw happening. Hannah longs for a child and has none. At the sanctuary in Shiloh she prays so hard, lips moving and no sound, that the priest Eli thinks she's drunk. She tells him she has "poured out my soul before the LORD." Eli sends her off in peace. And then the text says: "the woman went her way, and did eat, and her countenance was no more sad." Nothing had changed yet. No child, no answer, no news. But she had thrown it, and she ate her dinner. Last, the reason at the end of Peter's sentence: for he careth for you. The care you throw lands with someone who cares about you. In English it's the same word, care, going both ways.

Here's the practice: write a worry and hand it over. Settle, and breathe. Take a scrap of paper, or open a note on your phone. Write one worry in a few plain words. Look at it for a moment. Then do something with your hands: fold the paper and set it down out of reach, or close the note. If you pray, you can say the verse as you do it: casting all your care upon him; for he careth for you. If you don't, let the motion say: I don't have to hold this every second. The bell holds the time.
Cast your care. Throw your worry onto God, the letter of Peter says, because he cares for you.
Your line: he cares for you. Today, when the worry you wrote comes back, and it may, throw it again. Hannah went and ate her dinner. Eat yours. Day one thousand three hundred ninety-nine.

howItsDone: Christians bring worries to God in private prayer, in prayer journals and on prayer lists, and some churches keep prayer boxes or prayer walls where people leave written requests; 1 Peter 5:7 is often memorized and said in anxious moments.

fork.setup: you're Hannah. you've poured out your soul at the sanctuary, and the priest Eli has sent you off in peace. nothing has changed yet. what do you do?
options: keep fasting and weeping until something changes.
go your way, eat, and let the sadness lift.
fork.reveal: the woman went her way, and did eat, and her countenance was no more sad. she had handed it over before anything changed.

original.note: Greek: worry, anxious care — the 'care' you cast in 1 Peter 5:7.

trapdoor: what you thought: cast your care means stop caring.
what it means: throw the worry onto God, because he cares for you. you're sustained, not emptied out.
what a scholar hears: the two cares are different Greek words. merimna, anxious worry, is what gets thrown; the reason is that he is concerned for you.

notes: 'The same verb turns up in Luke' (ἐπιρίπτω in 1 Peter 5:7 and Luke 19:35): confirm. The lesson does not claim these are the only two uses.
Trapdoor: μέριμνα ('care', worry) vs. μέλει ('he careth') in 1 Peter 5:7 are different Greek words; confirm.
'Written to Christians going through suffering' rests on 1 Peter's own references to suffering (e.g. 5:9–10); confirm.
'The picture is older than Peter's letter' relates Psalm 55:22 to 1 Peter 5:7 without claiming direct quotation; confirm.
howItsDone mentions prayer boxes/walls and 'often memorized'; soften if needed.
